academic:
Alex Morgan

I study how institutions collect information and use it to organise public life. My research brings together social history, archives, and the history of technology.

My current work examines classification and comparison: how categories are made, how they travel, and what they leave out.

Dissertation

Classification and Public Life

2024

This study examines how rankings and categories shape institutions. It follows the movement from individual records to public comparisons, asking how measurement changes the people and organisations being measured.

The analysis considers the relationship between technical decisions and social authority: who defines a category, which differences it preserves, and what becomes invisible when records are reduced to a common scale.

Selected essays

Reading a Society through Its Records

2023

An examination of the ways information is preserved, arranged, and lost. Archives are treated as products of selection rather than complete accounts of the past.

The Work of Comparison

2023

A short essay on the assumptions required to compare institutions, and on the consequences of turning those comparisons into rankings.

Projects

The Writing Machine Archive

2024–2025

A digital exhibition tracing the development of mechanical writing across different languages.

The collection combines photographs, object descriptions, and archival material to explain how designers addressed scripts that could not be accommodated by a conventional alphabetic keyboard.

A Public Catalogue

2023–2024

An illustrated collection of objects and documents organised by their use, provenance, and historical setting.

Ironclads

Fleets, Trade and State Power

A study of naval power as an economic system: ships depend on finance, ports, supply networks, and the institutions that maintain them.

The material is organised around fleet construction, commercial routes, and the relationship between military commitments and available resources.

Fleet Records

Comparative notes on ships and the societies that built them, arranged as short entries with supporting references.

Blog

What a Strategy Game Chooses to Represent

18 September 2024

Historical games reach large audiences, but their rules select which parts of the past a player can see.

A useful reading begins with those choices. Combat, political institutions, and economic resources do not receive equal attention; each is translated into a different set of decisions. Examining that translation offers a way to discuss both the game and the historical interpretation it presents.

An Object Is Not Its Catalogue Entry

4 September 2024

A catalogue makes an object findable. It also compresses its history into a small number of fields. The gap between those two functions deserves attention.
